en: My inheritance, dearer than my father.
Broad-chested and shallow-maned,
He never flinched when ridden into battle,
Never tired when sent scouting,
His parrot-like tail trailing behind.
When a desert ninety days wide arose,
When people entered a land of suffering,
He endured every hardship.
My beloved Buurul,
I had him tended in a darkened stall
And had an amulet fastened around his neck;
When a dubious thing appeared,
The brass-beaked one tested and approved it.
Taybuurul, massive as a camel—
On high passes and sheer cliffs,
Buurul was the horse ridden over the heights;
In dire hardship and great battle,
Buurul was the horse ridden over the earth;
In blood-red slaughter and swirling chaos,
Buurul was the horse ridden on the flank.
Where lungs were split and heads were hewn,
Buurul was the horse ridden into the fray.
He guarded me like father and mother,
A beast as dear as one’s own father.
He never grew saddle-sore when ridden on campaign,
For he was a faithful companion.
Through the spreading enemy like a ship,
As though beholding Semetey,
His face grew pale and wan,
And blood flowing from both eyes
Poured down over his chest.
His joints gave way and he sobbed,
His courage fled and he wailed;
All twelve limbs and forty bones
Seemed shattered into pieces.
The horse remained, but its master was gone;
May such treacherous misery be damned!
Is this what you are, filthy world?
My soul is embittered, my heart is aflame.
I could mount Buurul and make him surge,
But my stallion-riding elder brother is not here.
His horse remains, but he himself is gone,
And a fiery ember has fallen into my heart.
My cheerful, lion-hearted brother is gone;
Is this what the filthy world is?
Grieving and lamenting, utterly distraught,
He wished to die but could not die,
Unable to take his own life.
Consumed by sorrow, his heart burned,
And he fell writhing into a wasting sickness.
As though his elder brother had returned that day,
As though God had granted his prayer,
The warrior stood weeping.
While Külchoro stood weeping,
The hard black stones melted and wept,
The broad-breasted earth wept,
And the sealed blue heavens above wept.
The watching multitudes wept,
The dark-hearted lion wept;
Everyone who wept
Wept while consuming his own grief.
If grief leaves a soul alive after death,
A beast has no tongue with which to speak,
Though it stands grieving like this:
The birches wept, the willows wept,
And every living witness wept.
The divinely favored lion wept,
The dark-hearted hero wept;
Everyone who wept
Wept while consuming his own grief.
When a helpless beast survives its master,
It must suffer so, they wept.
When poor Külchoro
Beheld Taybuurul,
It was as though his gray-maned elder brother had revived
And returned to reach his horse.
It was as though the dead gray-maned hero had revived
And his eyes beheld him today.
His face went pale and wan,
And the tears flowing down both cheeks
Poured over his chest.
Unable to hold back his tears,
Unable to take his tiny life,
He burned and baked to ashes,
Then faded from his embers into nothing.
When he beheld Taybuurul,
How could Külchoro, upheld by divine favor,
Possibly remain composed?
The reason he could not be still
Was that while his noble elder brother lived,
Over rugged hills and sheer cliffs,
This was the beast he rode along the ridges.
In battles between Chinese and Kyrgyz,
This was the beast he rode into strife.
With his fame spread throughout the world,
And his many conflicts ever increasing,
This was the beast he rode into battle.
He rekindled extinguished fires,
Restored those doomed to die,
Rejoined many who had been severed,
Regathered many who had been scattered,
And carried him safely far beyond the ravine.
Külchoro stands there crying out,
Calling for Taibuurul.
His senses gone, his heart aflame,
His whole heart burning as in fire,
He grieved in deep distress.
The dapple-gray horse he cherished
Was lost to him.
Over rugged hills and passes
The noble steed had gone.
Vanishing like a phantom,
The noble steed escaped.
However he looked, it could not be seen;
That wretched, accursed beast—
No one knew where it was.
Enduring hardship, grieving,
Parted from Taibuurul,
The tormented Külchoro
Stopped by a gateway rock
And lamented every sorrow of old.
In the yawning ravine
He poured out his regrets at length:
“When I rode the gray and made him rear,
And charged as though avenging a fallen hero,
When I donned my coat of mail
And leaned back as I struck the foe,
Why did I not die then?
When our vast wealth was safe,
When my gray-maned uncle lived,
When I crushed the Chymchyshkan
And held the frontier,
When I subdued Kakan
And put it to the torch,
Why did I not behold then
My true nature that never retreats?
I am stricken and grieving;
I have lost the one I cherished.
My lion uncle is no more,
And Külchoro has no fortune;
The noble gray he cherished
As dearly as himself is also gone.
When power slips from one’s hands
And beast and man alike wander lost,
When every living soul is seized
By wrath and grievous hardship,
Then days become like this.
When the yellow, hilly, sloping rocks
Become passes such as this,
When bleak days descend upon your head,
Then your people become like this.”
Clutching the reins, he wailed,
Sobbing and weeping in earnest.
“I girded the spear about my waist;
When seventy companies of foes came,
I charged alone among them—
Have I truly come to this?
Your back was made to ache,
Your flanks were rubbed raw,
Yet you never failed when ridden into battle—
Have you truly come to this?”
So Külchoro spoke,
And while he stood sobbing,
Before the words had left his mouth,
His heart cleft into ravines,
Then Taibuurul
Gathered in his belly and bounded,
Pounding the black earth.
The stars in heaven were eclipsed;
A dreadful wonder to behold—
He plainly escaped and fled.
Stretching his stride like an argali,
The noble steed brought shame upon them.
However they looked, he could not be seen;
No one knew where he was.
The noble steed vanished like a spirit.
When he lengthened his argali-like stride,
The creature had gone far away;
Vanishing, he had broken free,
The creature had departed.
However they looked, he could not be seen;
No one knew where he was.
“Crossing forty mountain passes,
Through terrible hardship and great turmoil,
The gray horse has fled.”
Thus Külchoro spoke,
His heart sinking and breaking,
His heart cleft into many ravines,
His cherished hopes shattered.
Aichürök and Külchoro
Both wailed and wept.
Dark clouds covered the sky;
This was a dreadful thing to behold:
The bloodthirsty hero’s noble gray
Plainly escaped and fled.
The gray began this calamity,
Appearing, then vanishing again.
Your gray-maned kinsman Külchoro,
Unable to endure such grief,
Was near to dying.
Brave Seytek grew impassioned
And set out upon Kylküröң.
The young prince’s fine son
Was himself a valiant hero.
Then brave Seytek said:
“My mother and my uncle—
If fate decrees, let me die,
But let me see where
My valiant mother Kanykei is.
If the cruel enemy Kanchoro
Has laid hands upon my mother,
I shall fight him and spill his blood.
I shall discover the truth.
If I do not return to my lands of Jylgyn and Keң-Kol,
To my renowned Kyrgyz people,
And settle in their dwelling place;
If I do not make my homeland
The ancestral land my father left,
Go and honor his tomb,
And send word to my people—
Ancient Talas and Keң-Koshoy
Are lands left by my forefathers.
He has none of his possessions left,
Nor the gray horse he cherished
In place of an elder brother.
Parted from the gray horse,
Külchoro has no fortune.
Ah, my valiant uncle, may you live;
May Külchoro never know misery.
May God, who creates the soul,
Never visit affliction like this
Upon His mortal servant.
Who has not tilted jauntily
The sable cap upon his head?
While fortune crowned his head,
Who has not gone about in thunderous pride?
When a valiant hero set his purpose,
What enemy before him did not scatter?
I fell captive and grieved,
Parted from my khan and uncle,
Whom I had held most dear.
While my valiant uncle lived,
I towered higher than the hills;
Parted from my hero,
I became more wretched than any man.
My head, once surrounded by followers,
Now reels as I grieve.
By my khan-uncle’s last command,
I have lost the noble steed.
While my fortune remained whole,
Ah, my dear one, I became a burdened soul.
Parted from my uncle,
Having lost the noble gray,
I have camped beside the river.
I have become embers from sobbing,
As though my fire had gone out.
